entries.1:1: God gave Jesus this message so his followers could know what is going to happen soon, and Jesus passed it on through an angel to John. It means the book comes from God and is meant to prepare you for what's ahead.
entries.1:2: John faithfully reported everything he saw and heard about God's message and Jesus. It means the writer is telling you this account is trustworthy and based on what he actually witnessed.
entries.1:3: God promises a blessing to anyone who reads this book aloud and to those who listen and do what it says, because the time is close. It means you are encouraged to read it, take it seriously, and act on it.
entries.1:4: John greets seven churches in Asia with a wish for grace and peace from God, who always exists, and from the seven spirits around his throne. It means this letter is addressed to real believers and comes with God's goodwill.
entries.1:5: Jesus is described as the faithful witness, the first to rise from the dead, and the ruler over earthly kings, and he loves us and washed away our sins by his blood. It means Jesus has real authority and has already dealt with your sin out of love.
entries.1:6: Jesus has made his people into a kingdom and priests serving God, and he deserves glory and power forever. It means you have a real role in serving God, and the credit belongs to Jesus.
entries.1:7: Jesus will come visibly with the clouds, everyone will see him, including those who pierced him, and people everywhere will mourn. It means his return will be public and unmistakable, and it will matter to everyone.
entries.1:8: God declares that he is the beginning and the end, the one who always was, is, and is coming, and the almighty ruler. It means the God behind this book is eternal and in complete control.
entries.1:9: John, writing as a fellow believer, says he shares in the hardship, the kingdom, and the patient endurance that come with following Jesus, and he was on the island of Patmos because of God's word and his testimony about Jesus. It means suffering for faith is something believers share together, not something you face alone.
entries.1:10: John was worshipping in the Spirit on the Lord's day when he heard a loud voice behind him like a trumpet. It means God can speak suddenly and powerfully when you are focused on him.
entries.1:11: The voice told John to write down what he saw and send it to seven named churches. It means the message was meant to be shared and preserved, not kept private.
entries.1:12: John turned to see who was speaking and saw seven gold lampstands with lights burning. It means the vision begins with a picture of something bright and valuable standing before him.
entries.1:13: Among the lampstands stood someone like a human figure, dressed in a long robe with a gold band across his chest. It means Jesus is present among his people, pictured as a priestly figure.
entries.1:14: His head and hair were white like wool or snow, and his eyes blazed like fire. It means he appears ancient, pure, and able to see right through everything.
entries.1:15: His feet gleamed like polished bronze refined in fire, and his voice sounded like rushing water. It means he is strong, pure, and his voice carries great power.
entries.1:16: He held seven stars in his right hand, a sharp double-edged sword came from his mouth, and his face shone like the full sun. It means he holds authority over his churches, his words cut to the heart, and his glory is overwhelming.
entries.1:17: John collapsed at his feet as if dead, but Jesus touched him and told him not to be afraid, saying he is the first and the last and the living one. It means even a terrifying encounter with Jesus ends in comfort and reassurance for those who belong to him.
entries.1:18: Jesus says he died but is now alive forever and holds the keys of death and the grave. It means death no longer has the final say, because Jesus controls it.
entries.1:19: Jesus tells John to write down what he has seen, what is happening now, and what will happen later. It means the book is organized to cover past, present, and future.
entries.1:20: Jesus explains that the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches and the seven lampstands are the churches themselves. It means the symbols stand for real congregations, showing that Jesus is paying attention to his churches.
entries.2:1: Jesus, who holds the churches and walks among them, is speaking to the church in Ephesus. This means he is present and paying attention to his people, including you.
entries.2:2: Jesus sees their hard work, patience, and refusal to tolerate false teachers. It means your effort and discernment are noticed by him, even when no one else sees.
entries.2:3: They have endured hardship for Jesus' name without giving up. It means steady faithfulness through trouble is something he values.
entries.2:4: Their problem is that they have drifted from the love they had for Jesus at first. It means it is possible to keep doing good things while your heart has grown distant.
entries.2:5: Jesus tells them to remember how they started, change their hearts, and return to their first works. It means turning back to him is urgent, because drifting has real consequences.
entries.2:6: They deserve credit for rejecting the practices of the Nicolaitans, which Jesus also hates. It means standing against wrong teaching is a good thing, even when other things need fixing.
entries.2:7: Jesus calls everyone listening to hear what the Spirit says, and promises life to those who overcome. It means the reward for staying faithful is real and lasting life with God.
entries.2:8: Jesus, the eternal one who died and lives again, is speaking to the church in Smyrna. It means the one addressing them has conquered death itself.
entries.2:9: Jesus knows their troubles and poverty, yet calls them truly rich, and he sees the slander they face. It means hardship and being misjudged do not mean God has forgotten you.
entries.2:10: Jesus tells them not to fear coming suffering, including prison and testing, and to stay faithful even to death. It means hard times are real, but faithfulness is rewarded with life.
entries.2:11: Jesus calls everyone to listen, and promises that those who overcome will not be hurt by the second death. It means ultimate safety belongs to those who stay faithful to him.
entries.2:12: Jesus, described as having a sharp two-edged sword, is speaking to the church in Pergamos. It means his words carry real authority to judge and correct.
entries.2:13: Jesus knows they live where Satan's throne is, yet they stayed true to him even when Antipas was killed. It means faithfulness is possible even in a very hostile place.
entries.2:14: Some among them hold to Balaam's teaching, which led people into idolatry and sexual sin. It means tolerating false teaching that pulls people into sin is a serious problem.
entries.2:15: Some there also hold to the teaching of the Nicolaitans. It means the same kind of harmful teaching was present among them too.
entries.2:16: Jesus tells them to change their hearts, or he will come quickly and fight those false teachers with his word. It means repentance is needed now, and he will deal with error.
entries.2:17: Jesus calls everyone to listen, and promises hidden manna and a white stone with a new name to those who overcome. It means faithful people receive a personal, lasting reward from him.
entries.2:18: Jesus, the Son of God with eyes like fire and feet like polished brass, is speaking to the church in Thyatira. It means he sees clearly and stands firm as he addresses them.
entries.2:19: Jesus knows their love, faith, service, endurance, and that their later works are greater than their first. It means growth in good works is something he notices and values.
entries.2:20: Their problem is that they tolerate a woman called Jezebel who claims to be a prophet and leads people into sexual sin and idolatry. It means letting false teaching go unchecked harms God's people.
entries.2:21: Jesus gave her time to change her heart, but she refused to turn from her unclean ways. It means God is patient, but patience does not last forever.
entries.2:22: Jesus will bring her and those who follow her into serious trouble unless they turn from her practices. It means continuing in sin brings real consequences.
entries.2:23: Jesus will judge her followers, and all the churches will know he searches hearts and rewards each person's works. It means nothing is hidden from him, and he judges fairly.
entries.2:24: To those in Thyatira who have not followed this false teaching, Jesus says he puts no further burden on them. It means he does not ask more of you than you can bear when you have stayed faithful.
entries.2:25: Jesus tells them to hold on to what they have until he comes. It means faithful perseverance is the task in front of them.
entries.2:26: Jesus promises that those who overcome and keep his works to the end will have authority over the nations. It means faithful endurance leads to sharing in his rule.
entries.2:27: They will rule with an iron rod and break nations like pottery, just as Jesus received authority from his Father. It means their future share in his authority is real and complete.
entries.2:28: Jesus promises to give the overcomer the morning star. It means faithful people receive a lasting reward that points to Christ himself.
entries.2:29: Jesus calls everyone listening to hear what the Spirit says to the churches. It means these messages are for all who will listen, including you.
entries.3:1: Jesus, who holds all spiritual power and authority over the churches, tells the church in Sardis that they have a reputation for being alive but are actually spiritually dead. It means a good reputation is not the same as real spiritual life, so the reader should examine whether their faith is genuine rather than just looking good to others.
entries.3:2: Jesus tells them to wake up and strengthen the little faith that is left, because their deeds fall short of what God requires. It means there is still time to turn things around, so the reader should act before what remains of their spiritual life dies.
entries.3:3: They are told to remember what they were taught, obey it, and genuinely change their hearts; if they don't stay alert, Jesus will come unexpectedly like a thief. It means the reader should not assume they have plenty of time to get right with God.
entries.3:4: A few people in Sardis have kept themselves spiritually clean, and Jesus promises they will walk with him dressed in white as a reward. It means faithfulness is possible even in a corrupt setting, and the reader can be among those who stay pure.
entries.3:5: Everyone who perseveres will be dressed in white, will never be erased from God's book of life, and will be acknowledged by Jesus before the Father and the angels. It means the reader's faithful endurance is worth everything, because Jesus himself will stand up for them in heaven.
entries.3:6: Jesus urges anyone who can hear to pay attention to what the Spirit is saying to the churches. It means the reader should take these warnings and promises personally, not just as messages for someone else.
entries.3:7: Jesus, described as holy, true, and holding the key of David with full authority to open and shut doors that no one can reverse, addresses the church in Philadelphia. It means the reader can trust that Jesus controls every opportunity and closed door with perfect authority.
entries.3:8: Jesus knows their deeds and has placed before them an open door no one can shut, even though they have only a little strength, because they have kept his word and not denied his name. It means the reader's weakness is no obstacle to God's work if they stay faithful.
entries.3:9: Jesus will make the false religious people who oppose them come and bow before them, so they can see that Jesus loves this church. It means the reader can trust that God will eventually vindicate those who are faithful to him, even when others falsely claim to be God's people.
entries.3:10: Because they have patiently kept his word, Jesus promises to keep them from the coming time of worldwide testing. It means the reader's steady faithfulness is noticed and will be rewarded with God's protection.
entries.3:11: Jesus says he is coming soon, so they should hold on to what they have so no one takes their reward. It means the reader should guard their faith carefully because the reward for faithfulness can be lost through carelessness.
entries.3:12: Everyone who perseveres will become a permanent pillar in God's house, marked with God's name, the name of the new Jerusalem, and Jesus's new name. It means the reader's future with God is secure and permanent, not temporary or uncertain.
entries.3:13: Jesus again calls anyone who can hear to listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches. It means the reader should take this message to heart as something the Spirit is saying to them too.
entries.3:14: Jesus, described as the faithful and true witness and the ruler over God's creation, addresses the church in Laodicea. It means the reader should listen to these words as coming from the one who is completely reliable and has authority over all things.
entries.3:15: Jesus knows their deeds and says they are neither cold nor hot, and he wishes they were one or the other. It means half-hearted, lukewarm faith is not acceptable to God, so the reader should be wholehearted rather than indifferent.
entries.3:16: Because they are neither hot nor cold, Jesus says he will reject them. It means the reader should take seriously that spiritual indifference can lead to being cut off from Christ.
entries.3:17: They claim to be rich and need nothing, but they don't realize they are actually spiritually wretched, poor, blind, and naked. It means material comfort can blind the reader to their real spiritual need, so they should not confuse wealth with spiritual health.
entries.3:18: Jesus advises them to buy from him true spiritual wealth, white clothing to cover their shame, and eye medicine so they can see. It means the reader should turn to Jesus for what they truly lack rather than trusting in their own resources.
entries.3:19: Jesus rebukes and disciplines those he loves, so they should be earnest and genuinely repent. It means the reader should see God's correction as a sign of love and respond with real change of heart.
entries.3:20: Jesus stands at the door and knocks, waiting for you to open. He does not force his way in.
entries.3:21: Everyone who perseveres will be given a place with Jesus on his throne, just as he overcame and sat down with his Father on his throne. It means the reader's faithful endurance leads to sharing in Jesus's victory and honor.
entries.3:22: Jesus calls anyone who can hear to listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches. It means the reader should receive this message as the Spirit's personal word to them, not just ancient history.
entries.4:1: John sees an open door into heaven and hears a voice like a trumpet inviting him to come up and be shown what will happen later. It reminds the reader that God opens the way for people to see and understand what he is doing.
entries.4:2: At once John is given a vision by the Spirit and sees a throne in heaven with someone sitting on it. It shows that heaven is real and that God is seated in charge, not distant or absent.
entries.4:3: The one on the throne shines like precious stones, and a rainbow like an emerald circles the throne. It tells the reader that God's presence is beautiful and glorious, and that his promise-keeping surrounds his rule.
entries.4:4: Around the throne are twenty-four other seats with twenty-four elders in white robes and gold crowns. It pictures God's people and leaders honored around him, showing the reader that faithful service is rewarded in his presence.
entries.4:5: From the throne come flashes of lightning, sounds, and thunder, and seven fiery lamps burn before it, which are the seven Spirits of God. It shows God's power and the fullness of his Spirit at work, reminding the reader that God is active and not silent.
entries.4:6: Before the throne is something like a clear glass sea, and around the throne are four living creatures covered with eyes. It pictures God's throne as pure and his creatures as fully watchful, showing the reader that nothing escapes God's notice.
entries.4:7: The four living creatures look like a lion, an ox, a man, and a flying eagle. These images suggest strength, service, wisdom, and swiftness, reminding the reader that all of creation serves God's purposes.
entries.4:8: Each creature has six wings and many eyes, and day and night they never stop saying that the Lord God is holy and rules over all. It shows that worship of God is constant and that he is worthy of it at every moment, including the reader's own life.
entries.4:9: Whenever the living creatures give glory and honor to the one on the throne who lives forever, something follows. It reminds the reader that God deserves praise simply because he is eternal and worthy.
entries.4:10: The twenty-four elders bow down before the one on the throne and lay their crowns before him. It shows humble worship, reminding the reader that any honor or position we have should be laid at God's feet.
entries.4:11: The elders praise God because he is worthy of glory, honor, and power, since he created all things and by his will they exist. It tells the reader that everything, including their own life, exists because God wanted it to, so he deserves their worship.
entries.5:1: God is holding a scroll that is completely written on and sealed shut with seven seals, meaning its contents are hidden and only someone with authority can open it. It shows that God holds the plan for what happens next, and it is not for just anyone to reveal.
entries.5:2: A mighty angel loudly asks who is worthy to open the scroll and break its seals. The question matters because opening it means being qualified to carry out God's purposes.
entries.5:3: No one anywhere, in heaven, on earth, or among the dead, was able to open the scroll or even look inside it. This shows that no created being has the rank or right to reveal God's plan on their own.
entries.5:4: John cries because no one could be found to open the scroll. His sorrow shows how much it matters that God's plan be revealed and carried out.
entries.5:5: One of the elders comforts John by pointing to Jesus, described as the Lion of Judah and the Root of David, who has won the victory and is able to open the scroll. Jesus is qualified because he conquered, so the reader can trust him with God's plan.
entries.5:6: John then sees a Lamb that looks as if it had been killed, standing in the center near God's throne, with seven horns and seven eyes that represent God's Spirit sent out over all the earth. Jesus is shown as the one who died and yet stands alive and fully empowered by God's Spirit.
entries.5:7: The Lamb goes and takes the scroll from the right hand of the one on the throne. Jesus is shown receiving the scroll directly from God, which means he is authorized to carry out God's plan.
entries.5:8: When the Lamb takes the scroll, the living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down before him with harps and bowls of incense, which are the prayers of God's people. This shows that Jesus is worthy of worship and that the prayers of believers are precious and presented before God.
entries.5:9: They sing a new song saying the Lamb is worthy to open the scroll because he was killed and by his blood purchased people for God from every tribe, language, people, and nation. Jesus' death was not for one group only but for people everywhere, so anyone can belong to God through him.
entries.5:10: The song says that those purchased by the Lamb are made a kingdom and priests to God and will rule on the earth. Through Jesus, ordinary people are given a high calling to serve God and share in his rule.
entries.5:11: John hears the voices of a vast number of angels around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders, counted in countless thousands. This shows that heaven's worship of Jesus is enormous and beyond counting.
entries.5:12: The angels say in a loud voice that the Lamb who was killed deserves power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing. Jesus' death, far from being a defeat, is the very reason he deserves all praise.
entries.5:13: Every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth, and in the sea joins in giving blessing, honor, glory, and power forever to God on the throne and to the Lamb. All of creation is meant to praise God and Jesus together, and the reader is invited to join that praise.
entries.5:14: The four living creatures say amen, and the elders fall down and worship. The proper response to who God and the Lamb are is wholehearted agreement and worship.
entries.6:1: Jesus, pictured as the Lamb, opens the first seal on a scroll, and one of the four living creatures calls out in a thunderous voice to come and see. It means God is beginning to reveal what comes next in his plan, and the reader is invited to pay attention.
entries.6:2: A rider on a white horse carries a bow and is given a crown, going out to conquer. This pictures a powerful force of conquest let loose on the world, reminding the reader that human power and victory are part of the story God is unfolding.
entries.6:3: When the Lamb opens the second seal, the second living creature calls out to come and see. The pattern continues, showing that each stage of the vision comes at God's command.
entries.6:4: A rider on a red horse is allowed to take peace away from the earth so people kill one another, and he is given a great sword. This pictures war and bloodshed as a real consequence in the world, and the reader sees that such violence does not escape God's notice.
entries.6:5: At the third seal, the third living creature calls out, and a rider on a black horse appears holding scales. The scales suggest weighing and measuring, pointing to scarcity and careful rationing of food.
entries.6:6: A voice from among the living creatures announces prices showing grain is very expensive, yet the oil and wine are not to be harmed. This means food is scarce and costly for ordinary people, while some goods are spared, so the reader sees hardship and want as part of what is happening.
entries.6:7: When the fourth seal is opened, the fourth living creature calls out to come and see. Again the vision moves forward at the command of God.
entries.6:8: A rider on a pale horse is named Death, with Hell following him, and they are given power over a fourth of the earth to destroy by sword, famine, disease, and wild animals. This pictures widespread death and suffering, and the reader is shown how serious the brokenness of the world is.
entries.6:9: At the fifth seal, John sees under the altar the souls of people who were killed because of God's word and their faithful witness. This means those who died for their faith are remembered and held close to God, giving the reader hope that such sacrifice is not forgotten.
entries.6:10: These martyrs cry out loudly, asking the holy and true Ruler how long it will be before he judges and avenges their blood on those living on earth. It means it is right to long for justice, and the reader is assured that God hears the cry of those who suffered wrongly.
entries.6:11: Each of them is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer until the full number of their fellow servants who will also be killed is complete. This means God comforts those who died for him and his timing for justice is not yet finished, so the reader learns patience and trust.
entries.6:12: At the sixth seal there is a great earthquake, the sun turns black like rough cloth, and the whole moon becomes like blood. These are signs of cosmic upheaval, showing the reader that God's judgment shakes even the heavens.
entries.6:13: The stars of the sky fall to the earth like unripe fruit blown from a tree by a strong wind. This pictures the created order being shaken, reminding the reader that nothing in the universe is beyond God's power.
entries.6:14: The sky is rolled up like a scroll, and every mountain and island is moved from its place. This means the familiar world is being turned upside down, and the reader sees that earthly security cannot last.
entries.6:15: Kings, rulers, military leaders, the rich, the powerful, and every slave and free person hide in caves and among the rocks. This means no one, however important or strong, can stand on their own when God acts, so the reader should not put ultimate trust in status or wealth.
entries.6:16: They beg the mountains and rocks to fall on them and hide them from the one seated on the throne and from the anger of the Lamb. This shows that people would rather be crushed than face God, and the reader is warned that resisting God leads to terror, not safety.
entries.6:17: They say the great day of God's and the Lamb's anger has come, and ask who can possibly stand. This means judgment is real and no one can survive it by their own strength, so the reader is urged to take God seriously and seek to stand with him.}}
entries.7:1: God holds back destructive forces on the earth until his plan is ready. It reminds the reader that world events are not out of God's control.
entries.7:2: An angel comes from the east carrying God's mark and calls out to the angels who bring harm. God sends his protection before judgment falls.
entries.7:3: The angels must wait to harm the earth until God's servants are marked as his own. God looks after his people before trouble comes.
entries.7:4: John hears the number of those marked: 144,000 from every tribe of Israel. The exact number shows God's people are fully counted and none are forgotten.
entries.7:5: The list of marked tribes begins with Judah, Reuben, and Gad, twelve thousand from each. God knows his people tribe by tribe and keeps a careful account of them.
entries.7:6: Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh each have twelve thousand marked. Each group matters to God, and none is left out of his protection.
entries.7:7: Simeon, Levi, and Issachar each have twelve thousand marked. God's care reaches every family and group among his people.
entries.7:8: Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin complete the list, twelve thousand each. The full number is reached, showing God's people are complete and secure.
entries.7:9: John then sees a vast crowd no one could count, from every nation and language, standing before God and the Lamb in white robes. God's saved people come from everywhere, not just one group.
entries.7:10: The great crowd shouts that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb. Rescue from sin and death comes from God, not from ourselves.
entries.7:11: All the angels around the throne fall face down and worship God. Heaven's proper response to God's saving work is humble worship.
entries.7:12: The angels give God blessing, glory, wisdom, and power forever. God deserves wholehearted praise that never ends.
entries.7:13: One of the elders asks John who the people in white robes are and where they came from. The question invites John, and the reader, to understand who these people are.
entries.7:14: The elder explains they are those who came through great trouble, their robes washed white in the Lamb's blood. Their standing with God comes through Jesus' sacrifice, not their own goodness.
entries.7:15: They serve God day and night before his throne, and God shelters them like a tent. God's presence is their home and their protection.
entries.7:16: They will never again hunger, thirst, or be scorched by the sun. God's people are promised an end to all suffering and need.
entries.7:17: The Lamb will lead them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear. Jesus personally cares for his people and ends their sorrow forever.
entries.8:1: When the last seal is opened, heaven goes completely silent for about half an hour. That silence is a tense pause, showing that something serious and solemn is about to happen.
entries.8:2: Seven angels who stand in God's presence are each given a trumpet. They are ready to act as God's messengers, and their trumpets signal important announcements to come.
entries.8:3: An angel stands at the altar with a golden incense burner and is given a large amount of incense to offer together with the prayers of all God's people. This shows that the prayers of believers are precious to God and rise before him.
entries.8:4: The smoke of the incense, together with the prayers of God's people, goes up to God from the angel's hand. Your prayers are not ignored; they reach God himself.
entries.8:5: The angel fills the burner with fire from the altar and throws it down to the earth, causing thunder, voices, lightning, and an earthquake. This signals that God's judgment is beginning and things are about to change.
entries.8:6: The seven angels with the seven trumpets get ready to blow them. The warnings and judgments they announce are about to start.
entries.8:7: When the first trumpet sounds, hail and fire mixed with blood fall on the earth, burning up a third of the land, the trees, and the green grass. It is a picture of severe judgment striking the natural world.
entries.8:8: At the second trumpet, something like a huge burning mountain is thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea turns to blood. This shows destruction spreading to the waters and the life in them.
entries.8:9: A third of the living creatures in the sea die, and a third of the ships are destroyed. The judgment reaches both sea life and human trade on the water.
entries.8:10: At the third trumpet, a great star burning like a torch falls from heaven onto a third of the rivers and springs. This brings the judgment close to the water people depend on for drinking.
entries.8:11: The star is called Wormwood, and a third of the waters become bitter, causing many people to die from drinking them. What should give life has been turned into something deadly.
entries.8:12: At the fourth trumpet, a third of the sun, moon, and stars are darkened, so there is no light for a third of the day and night. Even the basic order of day and night is shaken, showing how far the judgment reaches.
entries.8:13: An eagle flying overhead cries out three times 'Trouble' to everyone on earth because of the three trumpets still to sound. The worst warnings are still coming, so this is a call to take seriously what lies ahead.
entries.9:1: A star falling from heaven is given the key to the bottomless pit, the place of the dead. It shows that even the forces of darkness act only with permission from above.
entries.9:2: Opening the pit releases thick smoke that darkens the sun and sky. The scene shows judgment bringing confusion and darkness on the earth.
entries.9:3: Locusts come out of the smoke with stingers like scorpions. They are not ordinary insects but agents of harm allowed by God.
entries.9:4: The locusts are told to spare plants and harm only people who do not bear God's mark. God sets limits on who is hurt and protects those who belong to him.
entries.9:5: They may torment people for five months but not kill them, and the pain is like a scorpion sting. The suffering is severe but limited and controlled.
entries.9:6: People will want to die to escape the pain, but death will not come. The anguish is so great that death seems better than living.
entries.9:7: The locusts look like war horses with gold crowns and human faces. Their appearance is frightening and shows they are organized for battle.
entries.9:8: They have hair like women and teeth like lions. These strange features make them look both alluring and deadly.
entries.9:9: Their armor is like iron and their wings roar like chariots rushing to war. The sound alone would terrify anyone hearing it.
entries.9:10: Their power to sting people for five months is in their tails. The harm they cause is real but lasts only a set time.
entries.9:11: Their king is the angel of the bottomless pit, called Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, both meaning destruction. Evil has a leader, but he is still under God's authority.
entries.9:12: The first round of trouble has ended, with two more still to come. The reader is warned that worse judgments are ahead.
entries.9:13: A voice comes from the golden altar before God. The command for the next judgment comes from God's own presence.
entries.9:14: The sixth angel is told to release four angels held at the Euphrates River. These are forces kept ready until God allows them to act.
entries.9:15: The four angels are released at the exact time prepared for them to kill a third of humanity. Even destruction happens on God's timetable, not by chance.
entries.9:16: The number of mounted troops is two hundred million. The huge army shows the scale of the coming judgment.
entries.9:17: The riders wear armor of fire, smoke, and sulfur, and their horses breathe fire and smoke. The vision is terrifying and shows destruction coming from their mouths.
entries.9:18: A third of humanity dies from the fire, smoke, and sulfur coming from the horses' mouths. The judgment is deadly and comes directly from these creatures.
entries.9:19: The horses' power is in their mouths and in their tails, which are like snakes with heads. Harm comes from both the front and the back of these creatures.
entries.9:20: The people who survive these plagues still refuse to turn from worshiping idols and evil spirits. Suffering alone does not change hearts; people must choose to turn to God.
entries.9:21: They also do not repent of murder, witchcraft, sexual sin, or theft. Their stubbornness shows how deeply sin holds them, and the reader is warned not to be like them.
entries.10:1: A mighty angel comes down from heaven wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face bright like the sun, and his legs like fire. This shows God's messenger is powerful and glorious, reminding the reader that God's purposes are majestic and under his control.
entries.10:2: The angel holds a small open scroll and stands with one foot on the sea and the other on the land. This pictures his authority over the whole world, so the reader can trust that what follows concerns all of creation.
entries.10:3: The angel shouts loudly like a roaring lion, and seven thunders answer with their own voices. This conveys that God's message is powerful and demands attention, so the reader should listen seriously.
entries.10:4: John is about to write down what the seven thunders said, but a voice from heaven tells him to keep it secret. This shows that God does not reveal everything to us, and the reader should accept that some things remain hidden with God.
entries.10:5: The angel raises his right hand toward heaven. This is a gesture of taking a solemn oath, showing that what he is about to declare is serious and binding.
entries.10:6: The angel swears by the living God who made heaven, earth, and sea, declaring that there will be no more delay. This tells the reader that God's timing is certain and his promised judgment will not be put off forever.
entries.10:7: When the seventh angel sounds his trumpet, God's hidden plan will be finished, just as he announced to his prophets. This assures the reader that God keeps his promises and his purposes will reach their goal.
entries.10:8: The voice from heaven speaks again, telling John to go and take the open scroll from the angel standing on sea and land. This shows John is being directed by God to receive the message he must deliver.
entries.10:9: John asks for the scroll, and the angel tells him to eat it: it will taste sweet but turn his stomach bitter. This means God's word is pleasant to receive but its message of judgment is hard to bear, and the reader should expect that following God's word can bring both joy and pain.
entries.10:10: John eats the scroll, and it is sweet in his mouth but makes his stomach bitter. This shows that God's message delights at first but its serious content weighs heavily, reminding the reader that God's truth can be both sweet and hard.
entries.10:11: John is told he must speak again about the future to many peoples, nations, languages, and kings. This means his prophetic task is not finished, and the reader should expect God's message to go out to all kinds of people.
entries.11:1: God tells John to measure the temple and count the people worshiping there, which means marking out and protecting what belongs to God. For the reader, it is a picture that God knows and guards his true worshipers.
entries.11:2: The outer courtyard is left out and given over to hostile nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. This means God allows a set time of trouble, but it is limited and will end.
entries.11:3: God sends two witnesses who speak for him for 1,260 days, dressed in rough mourning clothes. It means God always has someone telling the truth, even in hard times.
entries.11:4: The two witnesses are pictured as olive trees and lamps standing before the Lord. This means they get their strength and light from God himself, not from themselves.
entries.11:5: Anyone who tries to harm the witnesses is destroyed by fire from their mouths. This means God defends his messengers, and attacking them is attacking God.
entries.11:6: The witnesses have power to stop rain and to turn water to blood and bring plagues. This echoes Moses and Elijah, showing God backs his messengers with real power.
entries.11:7: When their work is finished, a beast from the abyss attacks and kills them. This means even God's faithful servants can be defeated for a time, but only when God allows it.
entries.11:8: Their bodies lie in the street of the great city, called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified. This means the place that rejects God's messengers is the same kind of place that rejected Jesus.
entries.11:9: People from every nation look at the bodies for three and a half days and refuse to bury them. This means the world treats God's messengers with public contempt and shame.
entries.11:10: The people of the earth celebrate and exchange gifts because the two prophets troubled them. This means the world is glad when God's truth is silenced, showing how much it resists him.
entries.11:11: After three and a half days God's breath brings them back to life, and they stand up, terrifying everyone who sees. This means God's power is greater than death and will not let his witnesses stay down.
entries.11:12: A loud voice from heaven calls them up, and they rise in a cloud while their enemies watch. This means God publicly honors those who were publicly shamed for him.
entries.11:13: A great earthquake destroys a tenth of the city and kills seven thousand people, and the rest are afraid and give glory to God. This means judgment brings some people to respect God, even in fear.
entries.11:14: The second woe has passed and the third is coming soon. This means the series of judgments is moving forward toward its end, and more is still to come.
entries.11:15: At the seventh trumpet, loud voices in heaven announce that the world's kingdom has become the kingdom of the Lord and his Christ, who will rule forever. This means God's rule finally wins over all earthly powers, permanently.
entries.11:16: The twenty-four elders fall on their faces before God in worship. This means heaven's leaders respond to God's victory with humble praise, not pride.
entries.11:17: They thank the Lord God Almighty, who is and was, because he has taken his great power and begun to reign. This means God's rule is something to be thankful for, not feared by his people.
entries.11:18: The nations raged, but now God's wrath has come, along with the time to judge the dead, reward his servants and prophets, and destroy those who ruin the earth. This means God settles accounts fairly, rewarding the faithful and dealing with evil.
entries.11:19: God's heavenly temple opens, the ark of his covenant is seen, and there are flashes of lightning, voices, thunder, an earthquake, and hail. This means God's presence and promises are fully revealed, and his power shakes everything.
entries.12:1: This verse shows a symbolic picture of a woman in the sky, dressed in the sun and moon with a crown of twelve stars. It signals that a significant, God-given scene is unfolding, and readers should watch for what it represents.
entries.12:2: The woman is pregnant and crying out in the pain of giving birth. It shows that something important and costly is about to come into the world.
entries.12:3: A second sign appears: a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and crowns. It stands for a powerful, hostile enemy set against God's purposes.
entries.12:4: The dragon sweeps a third of the stars down and waits to destroy the woman's child the moment it is born. This shows the enemy's intent to stop God's plan before it can grow.
entries.12:5: The woman gives birth to a son destined to rule all nations, and he is taken up to God's throne. God protects and exalts the child, so the enemy cannot destroy him.
entries.12:6: The woman flees to a wilderness place God has prepared, where she is cared for during a set period of time. God provides and protects his people even in hard, hidden seasons.
entries.12:7: War breaks out in heaven: Michael and his angels fight against the dragon and his angels. This shows that a real conflict stands behind the troubles believers face.
entries.12:8: The dragon and his angels are defeated and lose their place in heaven. Evil does not win; it is driven out.
entries.12:9: The dragon is identified as the old serpent, the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world, and he is thrown down to earth with his angels. The deceiver is exposed and removed from heaven's realm.
entries.12:10: A loud voice in heaven announces that salvation, power, God's kingdom, and Christ's authority have come, because the accuser of believers has been thrown down. Believers can be confident that the one who accuses them before God no longer has standing.
entries.12:11: Believers overcome the accuser through the blood of the Lamb and their testimony, not clinging to their lives even unto death. Faith in Christ's sacrifice and faithful witness are what defeat the enemy.
entries.12:12: The heavens are called to rejoice, but the earth and sea face trouble because the devil has come down in great anger, knowing his time is short. Believers should expect fierce opposition, but also know it is limited.
entries.12:13: When the dragon realizes he has been thrown to earth, he attacks the woman who bore the male child. The enemy turns his fury on God's people when he cannot reach God's throne.
entries.12:14: The woman is given eagle's wings to fly to her prepared place in the wilderness, where she is fed for a set time, safe from the serpent. God gives his people the means to escape and sustains them.
entries.12:15: The serpent pours a river of water from his mouth to sweep the woman away. The enemy tries to overwhelm God's people with a flood of opposition.
entries.12:16: The earth helps the woman by opening its mouth and swallowing the river. God uses even creation to rescue and protect his people from the enemy's attack.
entries.12:17: Furious at the woman, the dragon goes to wage war on the rest of her offspring, those who obey God and hold to Jesus' testimony. When the enemy cannot destroy God's people outright, he targets faithful believers, so they should expect opposition and hold fast.
entries.13:1: John sees a terrifying beast rise from the sea, with ten horns and seven heads, symbols of great power and blasphemy. It warns the reader that a powerful, God-opposing force will arise and demand attention.
entries.13:2: The beast combines the strength and cruelty of a leopard, bear, and lion, and it gets its power from the dragon, which stands for Satan. The reader should recognize that evil power is real but borrowed, not ultimate.
entries.13:3: One of the beast's heads seems fatally wounded but heals, and the whole world is amazed and drawn to it. This warns that impressive recoveries and wonders can mislead people into following something dangerous.
entries.13:4: People worship the dragon and the beast, asking who could possibly match or defeat it. The reader is warned not to be swept up in awe of power that sets itself above God.
entries.13:5: The beast is allowed to speak arrogant words against God and to exercise authority for a limited period of forty-two months. Its power is real but temporary, and God sets its limits.
entries.13:6: The beast openly insults God, his name, and his dwelling place, including those in heaven. The reader should expect that opposition to God will be loud and offensive, not subtle.
entries.13:7: The beast is permitted to attack God's people and to gain authority over every tribe, people, language, and nation. Faithful believers may suffer, but this shows the beast's reach is allowed, not absolute.
entries.13:8: Everyone on earth worships the beast except those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life from the beginning. The reader is reminded that belonging to the crucified Lamb is what protects a person from deception.
entries.13:9: This is a call for anyone with ears to listen carefully. The reader is urged to pay close attention because what follows matters deeply.
entries.13:10: Those who imprison and kill others will face the same treatment, so God's people are called to endure quietly and faithfully. The reader should trust God's justice rather than take revenge.
entries.13:11: A second beast rises from the earth, looking gentle like a lamb but speaking like the dragon. The reader is warned that false teachers can appear harmless while leading people astray.
entries.13:12: This second beast uses the first beast's authority to make people worship the first beast, whose wound was healed. It shows how deceptive influence can push people toward idolatry.
entries.13:13: The second beast performs impressive miracles, even calling fire down from heaven. The reader should know that spectacular signs alone do not prove something is from God.
entries.13:14: The second beast deceives people through these miracles and tells them to make an image of the first beast. The reader is warned that deception often works through impressive displays.
entries.13:15: The second beast gives life to the image so it can speak, and anyone who refuses to worship it is put to death. This shows how far the pressure to conform can go, even to violence.
entries.13:16: The second beast puts a mark on the right hand or forehead of everyone, regardless of status or wealth. The reader sees that this system of control reaches every level of society.
entries.13:17: No one can buy or sell without the mark, which is the beast's name or number. The reader is warned that economic pressure can be used to force loyalty to evil.
entries.13:18: This calls for wisdom: the number of the beast is a human number, six hundred sixty-six. The reader is invited to think carefully and recognize the beast's identity rather than be fooled by it.
entries.14:1: Jesus, the Lamb, stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 followers who are marked as belonging to him and to God. It shows that God keeps and claims his people as his own.
entries.14:2: John hears a sound from heaven that is powerful like rushing water and thunder, yet also musical like harpists playing. It suggests heaven's worship is both awe-inspiring and beautiful.
entries.14:3: The 144,000 sing a new song before God's throne that only they can learn. It means those redeemed by God share a special closeness to him that others cannot fully share.
entries.14:4: These people kept themselves pure and followed the Lamb faithfully wherever he led. It means wholehearted devotion to Jesus is what marks God's people.
entries.14:5: No lie was found in them, and they are blameless. It means God's people are called to honesty and moral integrity.
entries.14:6: An angel flies across the sky carrying good news that is for every nation, tribe, language, and people. It means God's message is meant for everyone, without exception.
entries.14:7: The angel calls people to respect God, give him glory, and worship him as Creator, because judgment is near. It means now is the time to turn to God and honor him.
entries.14:8: A second angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen, the city that led the nations into corruption. It means the powerful systems that oppose God will not last.
entries.14:9: A third angel warns that anyone who worships the beast and takes its mark will face serious consequences. It means loyalty to evil carries a real and costly price.
entries.14:10: Such people will face God's full, undiluted anger and severe suffering in the presence of holy angels and the Lamb. It means God's judgment on persistent evil is real and serious.
entries.14:11: The torment of those who worship the beast never ends, and they get no rest. It means rejecting God to side with evil leads to permanent loss.
entries.14:12: This is where God's people need patient endurance, keeping his commands and holding on to faith in Jesus. It means believers are called to stay faithful even when it is hard.
entries.14:13: A voice from heaven says that those who die in the Lord are blessed and will rest from their labor, because their good works go with them. It means faithful believers can face death with hope, knowing their labor is not wasted.
entries.14:14: John sees someone like a son of man sitting on a white cloud with a gold crown and a sharp sickle. It pictures Jesus coming to bring in the harvest of judgment.
entries.14:15: An angel tells the one on the cloud to use his sickle because the harvest is ripe. It means the time for God's judgment has fully come.
entries.14:16: The one on the cloud swings his sickle, and the earth is harvested. It means the judgment announced by the angel actually takes place.
entries.14:17: Another angel comes out of heaven's temple, also carrying a sharp sickle. It shows that the judgment continues and comes from God's own presence.
entries.14:18: An angel with authority over fire calls out that the grapes are fully ripe and the vine of the earth should be cut. It means the wickedness of the world has reached its limit and judgment is due.
entries.14:19: The angel cuts the earth's vine and throws it into the great winepress of God's wrath. It pictures God finally dealing with the evil of the world.
entries.14:20: The grapes are crushed outside the city, and so much blood flows that it reaches the horses' bridles for about two hundred miles. It is a vivid picture of how vast and severe God's judgment will be.
entries.15:1: John sees a final, awe-inspiring scene in heaven: seven angels are about to carry out the last judgments, and with them God's anger against evil reaches its full measure. It reminds the reader that God does not ignore wrongdoing forever and that his justice will finally be complete.
entries.15:2: John sees something like a glass sea glowing with fire, and standing beside it are the people who stayed faithful to God and refused the beast and its mark. They hold musical instruments, showing that their hard struggle has turned into joy and worship.
entries.15:3: These faithful people sing a song that echoes Moses' song of victory and also honors Jesus, the Lamb, praising God as the all-powerful King whose works and ways are wonderful, true, and right. It invites the reader to trust that God's rule is good and worth praising, even when life is hard.
entries.15:4: The song asks who would not respect and honor God, since he alone is holy and his rightness has been shown to all. It looks forward to the day when every nation will come and worship him, giving the reader hope that God's fairness will one day be plain to everyone.
entries.15:5: John then sees the heavenly sanctuary, the place of God's presence and witness, opened up. This signals that something solemn and important from God is about to happen.
entries.15:6: The seven angels with the seven judgments come out of God's dwelling, dressed in clean, bright linen with gold bands across their chests. Their pure clothing shows that these judgments come from a holy God and are not cruel or random.
entries.15:7: One of the living creatures hands the seven angels gold bowls filled with God's anger, and God is described as the one who lives forever. This pictures God's judgment as measured and poured out from his presence, reminding the reader that he is answerable to no one and his justice is real.
entries.15:8: Smoke from God's glory and power fills his house so that no one can enter until the seven judgments are finished. This shows that God's presence is overwhelming and that his judgment must run its full course before anything else can happen.
entries.16:1: God commands seven angels to pour out bowls of his judgment on the earth. It shows that God is in control and his judgment is about to begin.
entries.16:2: The first bowl brings painful sores on the people who followed the beast and worshiped its image. Those who sided against God receive suffering instead of relief.
entries.16:3: The second bowl turns the sea into blood, killing everything in it. The judgment touches the natural world, showing how serious God's anger is.
entries.16:4: The third bowl turns rivers and springs into blood. Even the fresh water people depend on is affected by God's judgment.
entries.16:5: An angel declares that God is right and fair in these judgments. It reminds the reader that God's decisions are always just.
entries.16:6: These judgments are fair because the wicked shed the blood of God's people, so now they get blood to drink. It shows God does not ignore the suffering of the faithful.
entries.16:7: A voice from the altar agrees that God's judgments are true and right. It assures the reader that God's rule is completely fair.
entries.16:8: The fourth bowl brings scorching heat from the sun on people. The judgment intensifies, affecting daily life and comfort.
entries.16:9: Instead of repenting, people curse God and refuse to change their ways. It warns the reader that suffering alone does not soften a hard heart.
entries.16:10: The fifth bowl brings darkness on the beast's kingdom, and people are in agony. The beast's power is shown to be fragile under God's judgment.
entries.16:11: People still curse God and refuse to turn from their evil deeds despite their pain. It shows how deep stubbornness can go when someone rejects God.
entries.16:12: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates River to prepare a path for kings from the east. It sets the stage for the final gathering of forces against God.
entries.16:13: Three unclean spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet. These spirits represent deceptive influence that leads people astray.
entries.16:14: These spirits perform signs and gather the kings of the world for battle on God's great day. It shows that evil forces actively recruit people against God, but God remains in charge.
entries.16:15: Jesus warns that he will come unexpectedly, and those who stay faithful and ready are blessed. It encourages the reader to live watchfully and stay loyal to God.
entries.16:16: The gathered forces assemble at a place called Armageddon. It marks the location where the final conflict between good and evil will take place.
entries.16:17: The seventh bowl is poured out, and a voice from God's throne declares that it is finished. It signals that God's judgment is complete and nothing more is needed.
entries.16:18: Lightning, thunder, and an earthquake greater than any before occur. The whole creation shakes at the climax of God's judgment.
entries.16:19: The great city splits into three, cities of the nations fall, and Babylon is remembered before God to receive his wrath. It shows that no powerful city or system escapes God's justice.
entries.16:20: Every island disappears and the mountains vanish. The judgment is so total that even the shape of the earth is changed.
entries.16:21: Huge hailstones fall on people, and they still curse God because of the severity of the plague. It shows that even overwhelming judgment does not by itself produce repentance.
entries.17:1: An angel offers to show John the judgment of a corrupt woman symbolizing a powerful evil system, pictured as sitting on many waters. It means God will eventually call this corrupt power to account, so the reader can trust that evil does not go unjudged.
entries.17:2: The world's rulers and ordinary people have been drawn into her corruption and seduced by her desires. It warns the reader that this influence is widespread and can pull anyone into moral compromise.
entries.17:3: John is carried in the Spirit to a barren place and sees a woman riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, covered in blasphemous names. It shows that this evil system is tied to a powerful, God-defying force, so the reader should recognize the spiritual danger behind it.
entries.17:4: The woman is dressed in luxury and holds a gold cup filled with vile and impure things. It means her outward splendor hides inner corruption, warning the reader not to be fooled by wealth and glamour.
entries.17:5: Her forehead bears a symbolic name identifying her as Babylon the Great, the source of many corruptions on earth. It tells the reader that this is a mother-system producing widespread evil, so its influence should be resisted.
entries.17:6: John sees the woman drunk with the blood of God's people and those killed for their faith in Jesus, and he is stunned. It means this system violently opposes believers, so the reader should expect hostility but also know God sees the suffering of his people.
entries.17:7: The angel asks why John is amazed and promises to explain the secret of the woman and the beast she rides. It means God does not leave his people in confusion about spiritual realities, so the reader can seek understanding from him.
entries.17:8: The beast existed, then was not, and will rise from the abyss only to be destroyed, and those without God's life-book will be amazed by it. It means the beast's power is temporary and doomed, so the reader should not be dazzled by forces that seem impressive but end in ruin.
entries.17:9: The angel says wisdom is needed here, and explains that the seven heads are seven mountains where the woman sits. It means the symbolism points to real centers of power, so the reader should read carefully and seek wisdom rather than guess.
entries.17:10: The seven heads also represent seven kings: five have fallen, one is present, and one is still to come and will last only a short time. It means earthly political power keeps shifting and is short-lived, so the reader should not put ultimate trust in rulers or governments.
entries.17:11: The beast that was and is not is an eighth king belonging to the seven, and it heads for destruction. It means this evil power is both connected to earlier ones and destined to fail, so the reader can be confident it will not last.
entries.17:12: The ten horns are ten kings who have not yet received kingdoms but will share authority with the beast for a brief hour. It means allied powers against God are limited in time, so the reader should not fear their temporary strength.
entries.17:13: These kings are united in purpose and hand their power and authority over to the beast. It means evil powers can cooperate against God, so the reader should be alert to united opposition to what is right.
entries.17:14: They will fight against the Lamb, but the Lamb will defeat them because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and his called and faithful followers are with him. It means Jesus ultimately wins, so the reader can stand firm with him even when outnumbered.
entries.17:15: The angel explains that the waters where the woman sits represent peoples, crowds, nations, and languages. It means her influence reaches across many cultures and populations, so the reader should recognize how far-reaching this corruption is.
entries.17:16: The beast and the ten horns will turn on the woman, strip her, devour her, and burn her with fire. It means evil powers eventually destroy each other, so the reader should not envy or join them, since their end is self-destruction.
entries.17:17: God puts it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by uniting and giving their kingdom to the beast until his words are fulfilled. It means even hostile powers end up serving God's plan, so the reader can trust that God is still in control.
entries.17:18: The woman represents the great city that rules over the kings of the earth. It means the symbol stands for a dominant worldly power, so the reader should see through its grandeur and remember that God judges all such powers.
entries.18:1: A powerful angel comes down from heaven, and the whole earth glows with his brightness. This shows that God is about to act with full authority, and nothing can stop what he is doing.
entries.18:2: The angel announces that Babylon, a city that stood for human pride and evil, has fallen and is now a ruined, empty place full of unclean things. What looked strong and glorious has been brought down to nothing.
entries.18:3: The nations, kings, and merchants were all drawn into Babylon's greed and desire for pleasure, and they grew rich from it. This is a warning that joining in with a corrupt system pulls people into its downfall.
entries.18:4: God calls his own people to leave that corrupt system so they won't share in its sins or its punishment. It means the reader should not go along with what is wrong, even when it seems normal or profitable.
entries.18:5: Babylon's sins piled up so high that they reached heaven, and God has seen every one of them. Nothing evil is hidden from God, and he will deal with it.
entries.18:6: Babylon is to be paid back in full, even more than she gave, for the harm she did. This shows that God's justice gives people what their actions deserve.
entries.18:7: Babylon bragged that she was a queen who would never suffer loss, so her pain will match her pride. This warns that self-confidence and arrogance invite a sudden fall.
entries.18:8: In a single day disaster will hit her: death, grief, and hunger, and she will be burned up. The Lord God is strong enough to judge her, so her power cannot save her.
entries.18:9: The kings who shared in her evil will weep and wail when they see her burning. Their grief shows they loved what she gave them more than what was right.
entries.18:10: They stand far off, terrified of her punishment, and mourn that such a strong city was judged in just one hour. It shows how quickly human power and wealth can collapse.
entries.18:11: The merchants cry because no one wants their goods anymore. Their sorrow is really about lost profit, not about the evil that was done.
entries.18:12: The list shows the expensive things people traded: gold, jewels, fine cloth, ivory, and rare woods. These are the luxuries that made Babylon rich and that now mean nothing.
entries.18:13: The list continues with spices, food, animals, and even human beings treated as goods to be bought and sold. It shows how far greed can go, even to treating people as property.
entries.18:14: Everything Babylon longed for and enjoyed is gone forever and will never be seen again. It reminds the reader that pleasure and luxury do not last.
entries.18:15: The merchants who got rich from her stand far away, afraid of her punishment, and cry over their loss. Their fear shows that those who profited from evil are not safe.
entries.18:16: They mourn the city that was dressed in fine linen, purple, red, gold, and jewels. All that outward beauty could not protect her from judgment.
entries.18:17: In just one hour all that great wealth was wiped out, and everyone who made a living on the sea stood watching from a distance. It shows how fast riches can disappear.
entries.18:18: The sailors cry out in amazement, asking what city could compare with this great one. Their shock shows that no human achievement is beyond God's judgment.
entries.18:19: The sailors throw dust on their heads and mourn, because her wealth made them rich too, and now she is ruined in a single hour. Their grief is over lost riches, not over wrong done.
entries.18:20: Heaven and God's people are told to rejoice because God has judged Babylon on their behalf. It means God sees the suffering of his people and will make things right.
entries.18:21: A strong angel throws a huge millstone into the sea to show that Babylon will be thrown down just as suddenly and will never come back. Her end is final and certain.
entries.18:22: Music, skilled crafts, and the sound of grinding grain will never be heard in her again. All the ordinary life and work of the city will stop forever.
entries.18:23: Lights and wedding celebrations will never return to her, because her merchants ruled the earth and her lies led all nations astray. It shows that leading others into wrong brings serious judgment.
entries.18:24: Babylon is held responsible for the blood of prophets, God's people, and everyone killed on the earth. This means God does not forget the harm done to the innocent, and he will call it to account.
entries.19:1: A huge crowd in heaven shouts praise to God, saying that salvation, glory, and power belong to him. It reminds the reader that heaven celebrates God as the one who saves and rules.
entries.19:2: God's judgments are true and fair, and he has judged the evil woman who corrupted the earth and shed the blood of his people. It means God does not ignore injustice and will hold wrongdoers accountable.
entries.19:3: The crowd praises God again, and the smoke of the judged city rises forever, showing that her downfall is permanent. For the reader, it pictures evil being ended for good.
entries.19:4: The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fall down and worship God on his throne, agreeing with the praise. It shows that all of heaven joins in honoring God.
entries.19:5: A voice from the throne tells all of God's servants, great and small, to praise him. It invites every believer, no matter how important, to worship God.
entries.19:6: John hears a sound like rushing water and loud thunder as a great crowd declares that the Lord God Almighty reigns as King. It means God's rule is now openly recognized and celebrated.
entries.19:7: The people are called to rejoice because the time has come for the Lamb to marry his bride, who has prepared herself. It pictures the close, joyful union between Jesus and his people.
entries.19:8: The bride is given bright, clean linen to wear, and the linen stands for the righteous deeds of God's holy people. It means God's people are made pure and ready for him.
entries.19:9: John is told to write that those invited to the Lamb's wedding feast are blessed, and these words are from God. It means being part of Jesus' people is a true and happy privilege.
entries.19:10: John falls down to worship the angel, but the angel stops him, saying he is only a fellow servant and that worship belongs to God alone. It reminds the reader to worship God, not his messengers.
entries.19:11: John sees heaven open and a white horse whose rider is called Faithful and True, and he judges and fights fairly. It means Jesus is the trustworthy judge who stands for what is right.
entries.19:12: The rider's eyes blaze like fire and he wears many crowns, and he has a name written that only he knows. It shows his great authority and that there is more to him than anyone fully understands.
entries.19:13: His robe is dipped in blood and his name is the Word of God. It identifies the rider as Jesus, God's own message to the world, coming in judgment.
entries.19:14: The armies of heaven follow him on white horses, dressed in clean white linen. It shows that he does not fight alone but leads a pure and loyal host.
entries.19:15: A sharp sword comes from his mouth to strike down the nations, and he rules them with an iron rod and treads out God's fierce anger. It means his words carry the power to judge and his rule cannot be resisted.
entries.19:16: On his robe and on his leg is written King of Kings and Lord of Lords. It means he is above every other ruler and power.
entries.19:17: An angel standing in the sun calls all the birds to gather for a great feast God has prepared. It signals that a decisive judgment is about to fall on his enemies.
entries.19:18: The birds are called to eat the flesh of kings, commanders, strong men, horses, and people of every rank. It pictures total defeat for those who set themselves against God, with no one escaping.
entries.19:19: The beast, the kings of the earth, and their armies gather to fight against the rider on the horse and his army. It shows the world's powers openly opposing Jesus.
entries.19:20: The beast and the false prophet, who deceived people with signs and the mark of the beast, are captured and thrown alive into the lake of fire. It means the deceivers are stopped and punished for good.
entries.19:21: The rest of the enemies are killed by the sword coming from the rider's mouth, and the birds eat their fill. It shows that Jesus wins the battle by his word alone, and resistance to him ends in ruin.
entries.20:1: An angel comes down from heaven holding a key and a chain, ready to take control of a powerful evil force. It shows that God, not evil, is in charge of what happens next.
entries.20:2: The angel grabs Satan, described as the dragon and old snake, and chains him up for a thousand years. Evil is not free to do whatever it wants; it is limited by God's authority.
entries.20:3: Satan is locked away so he can't deceive the nations during the thousand years, but he will be released for a short time afterward. God sets the limits on evil, and even its temporary release is under his plan.
entries.20:4: John sees thrones with people judging, and also those who were killed for following Jesus and who refused to worship the beast. They come to life and rule with Christ for a thousand years, showing that faithfulness to God is honored even through death.
entries.20:5: The rest of the dead stay dead until the thousand years are over; this raising of the faithful is called the first resurrection. It points to a special hope for those who belong to Christ.
entries.20:6: Those who share in this first resurrection are blessed and holy, and the second death has no power over them. They serve God and Christ as priests and rule with him, which means their future is secure and honored.
entries.20:7: When the thousand years end, Satan is released from his prison. His release is temporary and happens on God's timetable, not his own.
entries.20:8: Satan goes out to deceive the nations all over the earth, called Gog and Magog, and gathers a huge army for war. Even after a long time of peace, people can still be led astray, so we should stay alert.
entries.20:9: The gathered armies surround God's people and the beloved city, but fire from heaven destroys them. God protects his people and defeats those who attack them.
entries.20:10: The devil who deceived them is thrown into the lake of burning fire with the beast and false prophet, to be punished forever. Evil finally gets what it deserves, and it will not trouble anyone again.
entries.20:11: John sees a great white throne and the one sitting on it, and earth and sky flee from his presence. This is God as the final judge, before whom everything else fades away.
entries.20:12: The dead, great and small, stand before the throne, and books are opened, including the book of life; they are judged by what they have done. Everyone will give an account to God, and what we do matters.
entries.20:13: The sea, death, and hell give up their dead, and each person is judged by their deeds. No one is forgotten or hidden; everyone will face God's judgment.
entries.20:14: Death and hell themselves are thrown into the lake of fire, which is called the second death. Death is not the end; it will finally be destroyed.
entries.20:15: Anyone whose name is not written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire. The book of life is what matters most, so being known by God is the thing to seek.
entries.21:1: God makes a completely new world, and the old one with all its trouble is gone for good. For you, it means the brokenness you see now is not the final story.
entries.21:2: God's holy city comes down from heaven, pictured as a bride beautifully prepared for her husband. It shows God's people are deeply loved and made ready to live with him.
entries.21:3: A loud voice announces that God will now live directly among people, and they will belong to him. For you, it means closeness with God himself, not distance.
entries.21:4: Every tear wiped away, death gone, pain over. The end of the story is not what it looks like now.
entries.21:5: God himself promises to make everything new and tells John to write it down because it is certain. You can trust this promise even when life still feels old and worn.
entries.21:6: God declares that it is finished, and he is the beginning and the end of all things. He offers life-giving water freely to anyone who is thirsty and in need.
entries.21:7: Those who stay faithful through hardship will inherit all these things and be called God's own children. For you, it means your endurance is not wasted.
entries.21:8: This verse lists people who reject God and warns that their end is the second death, a final separation from him. It is a serious warning to turn from such ways and trust God instead.
entries.21:9: One of the angels who carried God's judgments invites John to come and see the bride, the Lamb's wife. It shows the city is closely tied to Jesus, the Lamb.
entries.21:10: The angel carries John in the Spirit to a high mountain to see the holy city coming down from God. It means this vision is God-given and worth paying attention to.
entries.21:11: The city shines with God's glory, bright like a precious clear stone. For you, it means God's presence is the source of all its beauty and light.
entries.21:12: The city has a great high wall with twelve gates guarded by angels, each gate named for one of Israel's twelve tribes. It shows God's people are secure and that Israel has a lasting place in his plan.
entries.21:13: There are three gates on each of the four sides of the city. It suggests people can enter from every direction, and God's welcome reaches out to all.
entries.21:14: The wall rests on twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. It shows the good news about Jesus, taught by the apostles, is the firm foundation of God's people.
entries.21:15: The angel holds a gold measuring rod to measure the city, its gates, and its wall. It means the city is real and carefully planned by God, not a vague dream.
entries.21:16: The city is a perfect square, as wide and long and high as it is broad, measured at about fifteen hundred miles. Its huge size shows God's salvation is vast and complete.
entries.21:17: The wall measures one hundred forty-four cubits, a number tied to God's people. It pictures the city as perfectly secure and set apart for God.
entries.21:18: The wall is made of jasper and the city itself is pure gold, clear as glass. It shows the city's worth and purity come from God.
entries.21:19: The foundations of the wall are decorated with every kind of precious stone, starting with jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, and emerald. It pictures the city as beautiful and richly honored by God.
entries.21:20: The list of precious stones continues through the twelfth foundation, amethyst. Each stone adds to the picture of a city made glorious by God himself.
entries.21:21: Each of the twelve gates is a single pearl, and the streets are pure gold, clear as glass. It shows entry into God's city is precious and its life is pure.
entries.21:22: John sees no temple building in the city, because God Almighty and the Lamb themselves are its temple. For you, it means nothing stands between you and God anymore.
entries.21:23: The city needs no sun or moon, because God's glory gives it light and the Lamb is its lamp. It means God himself is enough to light and guide his people.
entries.21:24: The nations will walk by the city's light, and earth's kings will bring their honor into it. It shows God's saving work draws people from every nation.
entries.21:25: The city's gates are never shut during the day, and there is no night there. It means God's welcome and safety never end.
entries.21:26: The glory and honor of the nations will be brought into the city. It means the good things people make and do can be offered to God forever.
entries.21:27: Nothing unclean, false, or cursed can enter the city, only those whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life. It means being with God forever depends on belonging to Jesus.
entries.22:1: A clear, life-giving river flows straight from God and Jesus, showing that life and refreshment come from them. For you, it means the source of true life is God himself, not anything you must produce.
entries.22:2: The tree of life grows along the river, producing fruit every month and leaves that heal the nations. It pictures constant provision and healing for God's people, so you can expect lasting renewal from him.
entries.22:3: Nothing cursed or broken will remain, because God and Jesus will be right there with his people, who serve him. For you, it means the damage sin caused will be fully undone.
entries.22:4: God's servants will see him face to face, and his name on their foreheads marks them as belonging to him. It means you will know God personally and be known as his own.
entries.22:5: Night and need for lamps or sunlight will be gone, because God himself will be the light, and his people will reign forever. For you, it means unending life and honor in God's presence.
entries.22:6: The angel assures John that these words are trustworthy and come from the God who inspired the prophets. It means you can rely on what God has revealed about the future.
entries.22:7: Jesus promises he is coming soon and blesses everyone who takes this book's words to heart. For you, it means reading and obeying these words matters now.
entries.22:8: John, the one who saw and heard all this, fell down to worship the angel who showed him these things. It shows how overwhelming the vision was, and how easily even a faithful witness can misplace his worship.
entries.22:9: The angel stops John, saying he is only a fellow servant with John, the prophets, and all who keep this book, and that worship belongs to God alone. For you, it means keep your worship for God and treat his messengers as fellow servants, not objects of devotion.
entries.22:10: The angel tells John not to seal up the book's words, because the time for them to happen is near. It means these truths are meant to be shared and taken seriously now, not set aside.
entries.22:11: Those set in their evil or impurity are left to continue, and those who are upright and holy are left to continue too. It means a person's settled direction at the end stays as it is, so it matters which way you are heading.
entries.22:12: Jesus says he is coming soon and brings his reward, giving each person what their deeds deserve. For you, it means how you live now will be answered for when he comes.
entries.22:13: Jesus calls himself the First and the Last, the beginning and the end. It means he stands over all history and is the one who starts and finishes everything.
entries.22:14: Those who have washed their robes are blessed, because they have the right to the tree of life and can enter the city. For you, it means being made clean by Jesus gives you access to eternal life with God.
entries.22:15: Outside the city are those who practice what is corrupt, occult, immoral, murderous, idolatrous, or deceitful. It means such ways are shut out of God's city, so they are not to be toyed with.
entries.22:16: Jesus himself sends the angel to testify to the churches, and he identifies himself as David's root and descendant and the bright morning star. It means the one speaking is both the promised king and the light of hope.
entries.22:17: The Spirit and the church invite Jesus to come, and anyone who hears may join in, with anyone thirsty welcome to take the water of life freely. For you, it means the invitation to come to Jesus is open and costs nothing.
entries.22:18: Anyone who adds to the words of this prophetic book will receive the plagues written in it. It means treat God's revelation as complete and don't invent your own additions to it.
entries.22:19: Anyone who removes words from this book will lose his share in the tree of life and the holy city. It means don't cut out or water down what God has said.
entries.22:20: Jesus testifies that he is coming soon, and John answers with a prayer for him to come. For you, it means live ready and longing for Jesus' return.
entries.22:21: The book closes with a wish that the Lord Jesus' grace be with all God's people. It means everything ends where it began, with God's undeserved kindness toward his people.
